**Chapter 4**

The Drives That Went to Auction

*When old hardware leaves the building, who proves the data did not leave with it?*

In 2016, Morgan Stanley Smith Barney LLC (MSSB) closed two primary data centers, in Poughkeepsie, New York and Columbus, Ohio. The project covered about 4,900 devices, including 53 RAID arrays holding roughly 1,000 hard drives, plus about 8,000 back-up tapes (SEC order, paragraph 1).

MSSB gave the job to a moving and storage company. The SEC order calls it “Moving Company” and does not name it. The SEC said it had no experience or expertise in data destruction. The plan was for a specialist, called “IT Corp A” in the order, to wipe the devices. The contract called for certificates of destruction and asset disposition reports.

Early in the project, the moving company stopped using IT Corp A. Without telling MSSB, it brought in another firm, “IT Corp B”, which MSSB had not vetted. The moving company sold hard drives to IT Corp B, which understood the devices had already been wiped. They had not been. MSSB paid for wiping and degaussing that was never performed (SEC order, paragraphs 4 to 8).

Instead of certificates of destruction, IT Corp B issued “Certificates of Indemnification”. These only showed that IT Corp B had taken possession of the equipment and the risk of loss. The moving company emailed them to MSSB and called them certificates of destruction. MSSB did not review them (SEC order, paragraphs 6 and 7). MSSB never received a certificate of destruction for the 8,000 tapes. Its only proof was an email from IT Corp B, 18 months later.

On October 25, 2017, an IT consultant in Oklahoma emailed MSSB. He said he had bought MSSB hard drives on an internet auction site and could access MSSB data on them. MSSB bought back the drives he held. In June 2021, MSSB recovered 14 more drives from a downstream buyer. Forensic review of 13 of them found at least 140,000 pieces of customer personal information. The vast majority of the drives were never recovered (SEC order, paragraphs 9 and 11).

The problem was not limited to one project. In 2017, a certificate of destruction for 61 servers from Weehawken did not match MSSB's serial numbers (SEC order, paragraph 13).

Separately, MSSB's local branches used WAAS devices that stored fragments of data. In 2019, MSSB decommissioned 500 of them. In February 2020, it found that 4 were missing. In 2021, it found 38 more missing, 42 devices in all. The devices had encryption capability, but MSSB did not switch it on until 2018, and a manufacturer flaw meant older data stayed unencrypted (SEC order, paragraphs 14 to 17).

In July 2020, MSSB notified about 15 million customers.

In October 2020, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) assessed a $60 million civil money penalty against Morgan Stanley Bank, N.A. and Morgan Stanley Private Bank, N.A. The OCC said the banks “failed to exercise proper oversight of the decommissioning of two Wealth Management business data centers” in 2016, and “failed to maintain an appropriate inventory of customer data stored on the devices” (reported by Infosecurity Magazine).

On September 20, 2022, the Securities and Exchange Commission ordered MSSB to pay $35 million. MSSB did not admit or deny the findings. The SEC found that MSSB willfully violated the Safeguards Rule and the Disposal Rule of Regulation S-P. Gurbir S. Grewal, Director of the SEC's Division of Enforcement, said: “MSSB's failures in this case are astonishing.”

THE RECORD

- SEC order, Administrative Proceeding, Release No. 34-95832, September 20, 2022. Penalty $35,000,000. Censure and cease-and-desist. Findings on Rules 30(a) and 30(b) of Regulation S-P. Uses placeholder names “Moving Company”, “IT Corp A” and “IT Corp B”.
- SEC press release 2022-168, September 20, 2022. About 15 million customers. Failures from 2015.
- “Certificates of Indemnification” from IT Corp B, forwarded by the moving company to MSSB as certificates of destruction, 2016. Text not published.
- Email from the Oklahoma IT consultant to MSSB, October 25, 2017, saying he had bought MSSB drives at auction and could access MSSB data. Text not published.
- Weehawken certificate of destruction for 61 servers, 2017, with serial numbers that did not match MSSB records. Text not published.
- OCC press release NR 2020-134 and consent order, October 2020. Penalty $60 million. Read through a secondary report.

THE CHAIN

1. MSSB decommissioning project, 2016. Chose a moving company with no data destruction expertise. CONTROL POINT. The OCC said the banks “failed to adequately assess the risk of using third party vendors, including subcontractors” (reported by Infosecurity Magazine).
2. Moving Company. Dropped the approved wiping vendor and used an unvetted one without telling MSSB.
3. IT Corp B. Bought drives believing they had been wiped, and issued Certificates of Indemnification instead of certificates of destruction.
4. MSSB vendor oversight. Accepted the paperwork without reading it and paid for wiping that did not happen. CONTROL POINT. The SEC order says MSSB did not review the certificates (paragraph 7).
5. Auction buyers. Drives with customer data were resold online.
6. Oklahoma IT consultant. Reported the data to MSSB on October 25, 2017.

WHAT THE RECORD RECOMMENDS

- The SEC order requires MSSB to stop violating the Safeguards Rule and the Disposal Rule. Its findings point to what was missing: written disposal policies, vendor vetting, a certificate of destruction matched to serial numbers, and chain of custody.
- The OCC faulted vendor risk assessment and the lack of an inventory of customer data on the devices.
- In practice: keep an asset inventory down to serial number, require a certificate of destruction that lists each serial number, check it against your inventory, and turn on device encryption at deployment so that a lost drive holds nothing readable.

CAUTIONS

- The SEC press release says “42 servers”. The order says 42 devices (WAAS devices). Use “devices”.
- The SEC order does not name the moving company, the IT firms or the auction site. Do not name them.
- The SEC and OCC actions are separate. Do not add the $35 million and $60 million together as one fine.
- The OCC details come from a secondary report. The OCC site could not be read directly.
- The record does not show that the recovered data was misused. Do not claim identity theft or fraud.
- Do not name the Oklahoma consultant.

ELSEWHERE

- PSNI, August 2023: personal data published in a spreadsheet nobody checked (see Chapter 5). [4]

FROM THE COURSE DECK

- Slide 106: “Retention should be a deliberate, documented decision”
- Slide 115: “Data sanitization: clearing, purging, and destruction.”
- Slide 51, Supply Chain Security: “We can't directly control their security”
- Slide 51: “Use Contracts to Set Security Expectations”
